cells.tense: You're standing at the start of something and you already know which part of it is the real one.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you're starting, and the part of it you'd keep if you could keep only one. Say both out loud to one person today.
cells.core:
You're holding the first piece of something and not spending it yet. That's not stalling — it's the pause before the right investment, and you can tell which way it points. You arrive at it before the reasons do, and that order works for you.

What's working here is that you're not shoving the thing past where it actually is. The seed is in your hand. You can wait for the ground to be right without losing the shape of it. There's a cost to that waiting, and you're paying it without making it mean something about you. When you move, it'll move clean.
cells.sheetLine: You have the first piece and you know how to hold it.
cells.verb: starting something and holding its first form
cells.place: where you tell what matters before you can say why

cells.tense: You're already living three moves past the start, bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Set down one thing today that you've started mentally but not in fact. Leave it down until something real asks for it.
cells.core:
You've run ahead of the beginning. There's a first piece in your hand and you're already spending it, building the whole thing in your head, solving problems that only exist if you keep going the way you're going. The future you're steering toward can't be written in from here.

What that costs is the start itself. You can't begin a thing cleanly while you're braced against a version of it you haven't met. The pull is strong and it feels like direction. It's a grip. Coming back isn't more planning — it's letting what's in front of you be enough to act on, and finding out what it becomes instead of insisting on it.

cells.tense: There was a first piece in your hand, and you set it down somewhere you can't reach it now.
cells.ask: Pick up one thing you already have and do the smallest real thing with it today. Not the plan stage — something that changes its state.
cells.core:
You knew what mattered — got there before you could explain it. And then you stopped moving on it, and the not-moving has held. The beginning is still sitting there, untouched, while you wait for a certainty you'd only get by picking it up.

None of this is about whether you can see it. It's about acting on what you see before the act feels safe. Certainty doesn't arrive ahead of the doing; it shows up on the other side. Start with something small and real. You don't need the whole picture to lift one corner of this, and the rest comes into focus while you're in motion.

cells.tense: You're already choosing what to attend to and you're telling yourself it's just what's happening.
cells.ask: Point at one thing you've been treating as forced, and say out loud that you chose it. Once is enough.
cells.core:
You think you're being carried along, and you're not — you're the one weighing what gets your attention and what doesn't, and you've been doing it so fluently it stopped looking like a decision. When it goes well, it's plain: you look at what's in front of you, pick the part that counts, and put your weight there without needing to announce it. Something in front of you right now is a beginning, and you keep describing it as just the situation.

The direction isn't missing. What's missing is your name on it. When you say what you're choosing, it doesn't become a bigger deal — it becomes a smaller one, because you stop having to manage a story about how it isn't yours. The start is already running. You're just not signed onto it yet.
cells.sheetLine: You're already choosing this. You keep calling it the situation.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim in my draft is that the person can recognize the difference already; the record gives a capacity that precedes analysis, not evidence that it is currently succeeding at any particular decision. The reader could reasonably say 'I actually don't know what matters here and that's the whole problem.' If my read is wrong, the ask still works because it's a small act of naming, not a demand to feel certain—writing down what pulled at you is possible even when nothing pulls. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about essence or knowing-before-understanding landing on glass; I keep the mechanism and cut the vocabulary.
